description: A response is text somebody else wrote. Only request-derived values were sources, so data an application fetched from an upstream service arrived untrusted in reality and untainted in the engine -- which is why searxng's ~210 hostile-HTML-and-JSON providers had nothing to fire. The class is separate from request data rather than more of it, because what makes it worth reporting differs: a request is sent by a stranger and this is not necessarily, since an application routinely calls a service it operates itself, and the engine cannot read a URL and say whose host it names. So it declines to guess and narrows the DENIED SET instead, on measurement rather than on caution: widened experimentally to every context the first-order class denies, the policy added a console.warn, two build scripts and vendored WASM glue in pdfjs and one echoed Content-Type in linkwarden -- all of which turn on whose service it was -- and eight lxml parses in searxng, which do not. Four positives: a fetched field run through a shell, a fetched field interpolated into a statement, the same value arriving by framework dispatch at a SearxNG engine's `response(resp)` hook whose signature is the trust boundary because no resolvable call edge joins the framework to the module, and an upstream's XML through a parser that expands entities -- a pairing this model already asserts for a document a CALLER sent, and a parser does not care who wrote what it was handed. Two negatives that draw the line: a response written to a log is a log of what the upstream said, and a response handed onward to another service is an integration. The last handler is the other direction of the SAME call: a provider key presented under `params` is that provider's public configuration and stays silent, while an identically shaped key presented under `Authorization` is this program's credential and is reported. Seeding the answer changed neither reading, which is the point -- the two rules rest on the same fact about a third party and disagree about nothing.

expected.note: the positive control for the client-role rule: the same provider-issued shape as CATALOG_KEY above it, reported because the program files it under the request part reserved for proving who is calling

a field of the catalog's answer run through a shell. Low confidence because the path crosses `.json()`, which this frontend cannot resolve (ADR-005) -- the judgement is certain and the call graph is not
the same source interpolated into a statement rather than a command line; the destination is what names the weakness

the response arriving by framework dispatch. Not anchored to an enumerated entry point and reported below the gate, which is correct: a plugin hook is not a route, and the model says where the value came from without claiming a caller can reach it

eight searxng engine modules are this line, one per upstream that speaks XML. lxml's default parser expands entities and the call supplies no parser of its own; the only thing that differs from the caller-supplied case the model already asserts is who wrote the document
